prize_parts.citation: for developing methods to estimate demand and market equilibrium in differentiated-product industries, which made empirical industrial organisation a quantitative tool for competition and regulatory analysis

statement.case_for: I keep B005 first after reading the openings. The random-coefficients demand framework with endogenous prices, together with the dynamic industry models, turned empirical industrial organisation into a field where structural theory is taken to data in a transferable way. The methods are routine in merger review, antitrust and regulation, and they are used in trade, health and environmental analysis. That breadth of use across fields is the common criterion I apply to every ballot. The attribution is also cleaner than on most other ballots. Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes are the clear originators of the demand-estimation core, and Pakes also anchors the dynamic-industry strand. The work is about three decades old, with long validation and extension, so there is no timing concern. Two other candidates come close. B014 is a coherent, mature research programme with a clear three-person credit set. B027 has the cleanest attribution (Kiyotaki and Moore) and is clearly foundational. I keep them as alternatives, not as preferred parts.
statement.case_against: My strongest reservation is that this is a methods prize without a single headline substantive finding, and the committee may weigh that against discoveries from other fields. The three-name limit also forces exclusions. Bresnahan and Reiss shaped the earlier new empirical IO tradition, and Benkard and Levin are significant in the dynamic strand. Dropping them could look like favouring the estimation method over the broader programme. Sensitivity of BLP estimates to implementation choices and instruments is a real caveat, though it reflects mature scrutiny more than a flaw in the contribution.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B005 first but would credit Bresnahan alongside Berry and Pakes, on the grounds that Bresnahan led the new empirical IO tradition of inferring market power from data, which risks leaving out Levinsohn.
responses.response: I take the point that Bresnahan's contribution is distinct and historically important, and I am not certain that Levinsohn is the right third name. My view is that the citation should name one coherent discovery. Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes share the demand-estimation framework, which is the part of this field with the broadest reach beyond IO. Bresnahan's contribution is an earlier research programme about inferring market power, which suggests either a different citation or a broader prize than three names allow. I would not swap him in for Levinsohn without changing what the citation says. I remain open to that if colleagues argue the market-power-inference strand is the more central one.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B005 eighth. He sees the credit set as large and diffuse, asks whether the contribution is methodological rather than a discovery, and notes the sensitivity of BLP estimates to implementation and instruments.
responses.response: I accept that the credit set listed on the ballot is diffuse, but the three-person core is not. I also accept that implementation sensitivity is a real issue. I read it as evidence of three decades of scrutiny and refinement, and it has not displaced the framework. On methods versus discovery, I would not discount a contribution because its output is a measurement tool. The test I would apply is whether it changed what can be learned credibly about questions that matter for welfare and policy. For merger analysis and market-power measurement it plainly did. I would still not call it clearly stronger than the collateral-constraint mechanism on B027, which Boppart ranks first.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B027 first. He argues that the Kiyotaki-Moore collateral-constraint mechanism is conceptually original and widely influential, and that a two-person prize is the cleanest attribution.
responses.response: I agree that attribution on B027 is cleaner than on most ballots, and that the amplification mechanism is foundational. I rank it lower for two reasons. Krusell and others note that direct empirical identification of the mechanism is more contested than the theory. There is also partial overlap with the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises. B005 has an unusually strong record of validation in practice and wider use outside its home field. This is a weighing of criteria, not a claim that B027 is weak, and I list it as an alternative.

responses.point: Strömberg ranks B005 first and rates the demand-side attribution as clean. He also ranks B036 second, where he sees the credit as spread across many people.
responses.response: I agree on B005. On B036 I read the same diffuse attribution as a larger obstacle than he does, and I ranked it last in my opening. Eight credited names cannot be reduced to three without contested omissions of Gali, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Gertler and Smets. Even a defensible trio would invite a dispute over who is left out. That attribution problem is a stronger objection to B036 than it is to B005, and I would not use B036's very large policy impact to offset it.

uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers to credit Bresnahan or Reiss for the broader empirical-IO tradition over Levinsohn, and whether that would change the citation wording.
Whether a prize on methods is judged to rank below substantive discoveries from other fields.
How much weight to give B014 and B027 relative to B005 given their potential overlap with the 2024 and 2022 prizes, which I cannot settle from the evidence supplied.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My research is in market and mechanism design (matching, auctions, fair allocation), and none of my listed collaborators or affiliations appear among the credited names on B005, B014 or B027. I disclose that I am a member of the simulated committee and an SSE affiliate with some colleagues, but I do not read this as a conflict.
